target_claim: For an arbitrary edge e in T1 with components A,B of T1\{e}, choosing ANY edge f of T2 crossing the (A,B) cut makes both (T1\{e})+f and (T2\{f})+e trees; in particular (V,(T2\{f})+e) is claimed to be a tree.
source_quote:
there must exist at least one edge f in T2 that connects a vertex in A to
a vertex in B. Choose any such edge f.
...
Therefore (V, (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e}) is a tree.
test_sketch: Implement the stated procedure: remove e from T1, BFS to get components A,B, enumerate T2 edges crossing the cut, pick an arbitrary one f (e.g., the last in edge order), form (T2\{f})+e and check tree-ness (n-1 edges, connected, acyclic) with a brute-force checker. Input family: all pairs of labeled trees on n<=6 vertices (or random pairs, n<=12) and each e in T1, trying every crossing f. Concrete failing instance: V={1,2,3,4}, T1={12,23,34}, e={2,3} so A={1,2},B={3,4}; T2={12,13,14}; crossing edge f={1,4} gives (T2\{f})+e={12,13,23}, which has cycle 1-2-3 and isolated vertex 4 - the oracle reports not-a-tree, refuting line 0027's claim for 'any such edge f'.
